text: Which is the strongest argument against reflection in ordinary application code?
choices: It requires catching three checked exceptions, which makes the code verbose.
The module system will eventually forbid it, so such code has no future.
It is forty to sixty times slower than a direct call, which no program can afford.
Every compile-time check is suspended — a misspelled name becomes a run-time exception, and renaming in an IDE misses it.
explanation: The speed cost is real and usually irrelevant; the safety cost is not. It also breaks find-usages, dead-code elimination, obfuscation, and ahead-of-time compilation — which is why the ecosystem has spent years moving reflective work to compile-time code generation. The rule: if you know the class at compile time, call the method.
